money_at_stake.rationale: No source found this run prices 'the compliance-verification and data-center-requalification chain' as its own line item, so this leg is sized on the two closest cited pools rather than an invented figure. The Southeast Asia data-center colocation market, the physical capacity that has to requalify its tenant base under this enforcement mechanism, is valued at USD 5.76 billion in 2025, projected to reach USD 13.69 billion by 2031 at a 15.5% CAGR. Individual transactions inside that market already run into the billions: Megaspeed alone purchased nearly USD 2 billion worth of advanced Nvidia chips through its Malaysian subsidiary before being ejected from its hosting hub. Both figures sit inside B1_10; neither approaches B10_100.

public_reach.rationale: Structurally thin, and the signal card's own retail_gap already flags why: the only large listed name anywhere in this story is Nvidia, and Nvidia is a pass-through, the seller of the chip before it crosses into the compliance-and-requalification layer this occurrence is actually about, not the party whose money is directly at stake in verifying end users or requalifying colocation capacity. Every named operative company on the enforcement side is confirmed private this run: Megaspeed is a Singapore-based firm spun off from a Chinese gaming firm, and Bridge Data Centers is a Bain Capital portfolio operation, neither listed. No source found this run named a single listed compliance-verification vendor, KYC/screening-tooling provider, or Southeast Asian colocation operator as a public company capturing this specific mechanism. Scored at 28 rather than 15 only because Nvidia's own compliance operation (screening customer data centers, reviewing contracts, per FT reporting relayed in the card's own evidence) is at least real activity inside a listed company's cost structure, even though it is not priced as revenue anywhere found this run.

capture_odds.rationale: Too early and too contested to score as concentrated capture. The regulated act itself (remote/rental access) is still being drafted, not yet in force, so no company has a demonstrated, priced position enforcing or profiting from it; the House's Remote Access Security Act passed 369-22 in January 2026 and remains stalled in the Senate more than seven months later, and BIS's own rule is only expected to reach industry stakeholders 'as early as September.' The one confirmed operational dynamic, Nvidia auditing customer data centers, reviewing contracts and interviewing end users, is a cost Nvidia bears to protect its existing chip-sale revenue, not a new fee-generating position for a listed issuer. Even the underlying factual predicate is unsettled: BigGo Finance's own reporting states plainly that no public evidence, such as access logs or server ownership records, has yet been presented for the specific Thailand infrastructure allegation this rule is partly justified by. Scored at 28 rather than lower because a real enforcement precedent already happened (Megaspeed's ejection), which is more than a purely hypothetical mechanism.

timing_fit.rationale: Real and already moving, not merely proposed: BIS issued its remote-access guidance 2026-05-31 (this appraisal's anchor), a live enforcement action already occurred (Megaspeed's April 2026 ejection from Bridge Data Centers), and a formal rule is expected to reach industry as early as September 2026, all inside the current year. That is a fast-moving mechanism squarely inside the 2-5 year window. Held at 70 rather than higher because the rule that would make this durable and comprehensive (BIS's drafted remote-access rule) is not yet finalized, and its legislative backstop (the Remote Access Security Act) has sat in the Senate for more than seven months with no confirmed timeline, so the multi-year compliance-infrastructure buildout this occurrence's thesis depends on is credible and already starting rather than fully committed and dated.
